title: Jagsher Singh Khangurra Saves Match Point, Assures India World Juniors Medal
excerpt: The 17-year-old from Nabha rallied past Yuan-Syue Jhuang in three games in Cairo to reach the BWF World Junior Championships semifinals — and become the ninth Indian boys' singles player to podium at the event.
body:
• India's Jagsher Singh Khangurra saved a match point and rallied from a game down to beat Chinese Taipei's Yuan-Syue Jhuang 6-15, 17-15, 15-12 in the BWF World Junior Championships quarterfinals in Cairo, assuring India of a medal.
  • The 17-year-old from Nabha, Punjab, seeded 14th, won two matches on Thursday, including a 15-8, 15-8 pre-quarterfinal win over Malaysia's Lee Qian Chong.
  • Khangurra becomes the ninth Indian boys' singles player to reach the podium at the World Juniors; India have won one gold, five silver and six bronze in the event's history.
  • He next faces Indonesia's 31st seed Radithya Bayu Wardhana in the semifinals, with a place in the final at stake.

Jagsher Singh Khangurra assured India of a medal at the BWF World Junior Championships in Cairo on Thursday, saving a match point in the second game before completing a 6-15, 17-15, 15-12 comeback against Chinese Taipei's Yuan-Syue Jhuang in the quarterfinals, according to NDTV Sports. The win puts the 17-year-old from Punjab into the boys' singles semifinals and guarantees him at least a bronze.

The quarterfinal, played at the Cairo International Stadium, lasted 48 minutes, IANS reported. Khangurra had been two points from defeat in the second game before holding his nerve to level the match and then close out the decider. It was his second win of a demanding Thursday: earlier in the day he had beaten Malaysia's Lee Qian Chong 15-8, 15-8 in the pre-quarterfinals.

A run built round by round

Khangurra's path to the medal rounds ran through the draw's depth. In the round of 32 he defeated Thailand's 22nd seed Punnatat Prempunpong, and in the earlier rounds he beat Mauritius' Pranav Bhaugeerothee and Algeria's Mohamed Rayane Bouffeniche. Seeded 14th, he has beaten a higher seed and saved his best recovery for the match that decided the medals.

The result makes Khangurra the ninth boys' singles player from India to finish on the podium at the World Junior Championships, according to IANS. India have so far won one gold, five silver and six bronze medals at the championships. He has won six medals at international tournaments in his young career.

From Nabha to Bengaluru

Khangurra hails from Nabha town near Patiala in Punjab, where both his parents work as government school teachers; he is the first in his family to take up badminton, having picked up the sport at seven and left home at 11 to train. After initial coaching at an academy in Bahadurgarh and a stint at the Uday Pawar Academy in Mumbai, he has spent the past two years at the Centre for Badminton Excellence in Bengaluru under former national coach Vimal Kumar, IANS reported.

The grounding shows in his record. A former under-17 national champion and Asian medallist in his age group, he first drew attention with a medal at the under-15 nationals two years ago, reached No. 1 in the national under-17 boys' singles rankings in January 2026, and was ranked eighth in the under-19 section as of September 22, 2026.

A mixed day for the rest of the Indian squad

Khangurra's win was the bright spot of a mixed day for India, RevSportz reported. In the girls' singles, Shaina Manimuthu — an Asian under-17 silver medallist — beat Japan's Yurika Nagafuchi in the round of 16 but lost her quarterfinal to China's Yi Qing Yin 5-15, 8-15, one win short of a medal. Tanvi Patri and Tanvi Reddy Andluri also exited in the round of 16. In the boys' singles, Dev Ruparelia lost a close three-game match to Hong Kong's Chan Yee Hei, and Nishchal Chand fell to Indonesia's Fardhan Rainanda Joe. India's pairs in the girls' and boys' doubles were also beaten in their matches.

What comes next

Khangurra now faces Indonesia's Radithya Bayu Wardhana, the 31st seed, in the semifinals, with the winner advancing to the final. A semifinal win would lift India's guaranteed medal from bronze to at least silver and give Khangurra a shot at adding to the single gold in India's World Juniors history. Whatever the colour, a medal at his first World Junior Championships — won by saving a match point — marks him as one of the names to track as India's next junior cohort moves toward the senior circuit.
